cards.q: What is the Modular QoS CLI (MQC)?
cards.a: MQC is the standard Cisco QoS framework that separates QoS into three building blocks: class-map to match traffic, policy-map to define the treatment, and service-policy to attach them to an interface.

cards.q: What are the three MQC building blocks and their commands?
cards.a: class-map (match traffic), policy-map (define treatment), and service-policy (attach to an interface in the input or output direction).

cards.q: What is the difference between match-all and match-any in a class-map?
cards.a: match-all requires every criterion in the class-map to match, while match-any lets the packet match if any single criterion matches.

cards.q: What are common class-map match commands?
cards.a: match dscp, match access-group, match ip precedence, match cos, and match protocol for NBAR application-level matching.

cards.q: What are the main policy-map action commands?
cards.a: set dscp/set cos/set precedence for marking, police for rate enforcement, shape for smoothing, bandwidth for CBWFQ, priority for LLQ, queue-limit, random-detect for WRED, and fair-queue for per-flow scheduling.

cards.q: How is a policy-map attached to an interface?
cards.a: With the command service-policy input NAME or service-policy output NAME; a policy is attached in only one direction (input or output).
It is the implicit catch-all class that matches all traffic not matched by any other class in a policy-map, used for default behavior such as shaping or queuing.
It nests a child policy-map inside a parent policy using a service-policy statement, so the parent shapes the aggregate rate while the child applies per-class sub-treatments.

cards.q: Which commands verify MQC policy and class state?
cards.a: show class-map, show policy-map, and show policy-map interface.

cards.q: A QoS policy has no effect on traffic; what is the likely cause?
cards.a: The policy-map was never attached with service-policy, or it was attached in the wrong direction (input vs output); verify the interface attach with show policy-map interface.

cards.q: What is the key exam distinction among the three MQC blocks?
cards.a: class-map matches (what), policy-map acts (how), and service-policy attaches (where and in which direction); confusing these three is a common mistake.

cards.q: What is the MQC quick-review summary?
cards.a: MQC uses class-map to match (match-all vs match-any), policy-map to apply actions (set, police, shape, priority, bandwidth), and service-policy input/output to attach, with class-default catching unmatched traffic and parent/child policies for hierarchy.
